summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, diabetes, gastroparesis, bipolar disorder, and recent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and appendectomy presented with syncope, reported seizure-like activity, and persistent right-sided abdominal pain with vomiting and fever. He was admitted for evaluation and management. Imaging showed no acute intracranial pathology, a small postoperative fluid collection, and mild bile duct dilation without retained stones. He was managed with IV fluids, pain control via PCA, and transitioned to oral medications. He experienced transient hallucinations, likely due to hospital stress and pain, which resolved with low-dose Haldol. His symptoms improved, he tolerated oral intake, and was discharged home in stable condition with follow-up plans for surgery, neurology, and psychiatry, and instructions to monitor for warning signs of complications.
